lead: Gear teeth are made by copying the tooth space or by generating the involute. Copying uses a form cutter shaped to the gap; generating uses a cutter and workpiece driven in a fixed ratio so the involute appears as a trace. The first is simple but needs many cutters; the second is fast and accurate and is standard for spur and helical gears. Gearboxes in scooters, pumps, lathe headstocks and industrial drives use these methods. This chapter covers gear terms, forming, hobbing, shaping, rack planning and a dividing-head check.
prereq: You need: 5.7 for milling cutters and simple indexing; the involute idea from geometry.

blocks.text: Spur gear size is fixed by module m (mm) and tooth count z. Module is the pitch diameter per tooth: m = d/z, so pitch diameter d = mz. Circular pitch p = πm is the arc from one tooth to the next on the pitch circle. Addendum is m above the pitch circle; dedendum is 1.25m below it. Outside diameter is d + 2m. These values set cutter depth and blank diameter.

Forming copies the gap between two teeth. A form milling cutter has the inverse tooth profile; it is fed along the blank and the blank is indexed one pitch between cuts. A broach does the same with a long stepped tool that cuts all teeth in one stroke, mainly for internal gears or large batches. The cutter number depends on tooth count. The involute changes with z, so one cutter cannot cut every gear correctly; a set covers ranges, and the nearest number is chosen. Some syllabi call this copy milling.

Forming suits repair shops, small batches and gears where a suitable cutter exists. It leaves indexing marks and cutter profile error. A low-speed gear may pass, but a continuously running gearbox needs generated teeth.

Generation does not copy the gap. A cutter and workpiece rotate in a fixed ratio, and the cutter edges sweep the involute. Hobbing uses a hob: a worm with gashes that form cutting edges. The hob axis is tilted by its lead angle; hob and blank rotate as a worm and gear pair. Axial feed moves the hob along the blank to cut the full face width; radial feed plunges to full depth. In conventional hobbing the cutter rotation opposes the feed; in climb hobbing it runs with the feed, giving thinner chips and better finish on rigid machines. Both are hobbing types; axial and radial are feed directions, not the same classification.

Gear shaping uses a pinion-shaped cutter. It reciprocates along the tooth and rotates with the work in the correct ratio; the involute is generated by the rolling motion. It reaches close shoulders and internal gears. Rack planning uses a rack-shaped cutter that reciprocates while the work rotates; the straight rack flank generates the involute. Only a few universities teach rack planning in detail. Generation is faster and more accurate than forming for production, but the machine setting must be exact.

Use forming for one-off repair, large module, or when no hob is available. Use generation for batch production of spur and helical gears. Forming leaves indexing marks and cutter profile error; generation gives smooth spacing because the same rolling motion repeats each tooth. A form-milled gear can pass a low-speed duty, but a gearbox that runs continuously needs generated teeth. Powder metallurgy can mould small gears without cutting; it is an alternative covered in Unit 2. Hardened gears are finished by grinding or honing, covered in 5.9.

The choice also depends on gear type. External spur and helical gears are usually hobbed; internal gears and close shoulders favour shaping. Rack planning is mainly a teaching method for the involute, not a common production route. In the shop, the first check is module and tooth count, then the machine setup, cutter number for forming, and the index plate for milling. A wrong module is a scrap gear, not a small error.

examples.question: A 30-tooth spur gear of module 3 mm is to be cut on a milling machine with a simple dividing head of ratio 40:1. Find pitch diameter, circular pitch, addendum, dedendum, outside diameter, and the indexing crank turns. Choose a 24-hole circle.
steps: Given tooth count z = 30, module m = 3 mm, dividing-head ratio R = 40 crank turns per work turn, hole circle H = 24 holes.
Circular pitch p = πm = π × 3 = 9.425 mm.
Crank turns per tooth = R/z = 40/30 = 1.333 turn. The fraction is 1/3 turn. On a 24-hole circle, holes = (1/3) × 24 = 8 holes. So use 1 full turn plus 8 holes.
examples.answer: The gear has pitch diameter 90 mm, circular pitch 9.425 mm, addendum 3 mm, dedendum 3.75 mm, outside diameter 96 mm, and indexing crank turns 1.333 turn, that is 1 turn plus 8 holes on a 24-hole circle.
examples.check:
import math
z = 30
m = 3
R = 40
H = 24
d = m * z
p = math.pi * m
a = m
b = 1.25 * m
da = d + 2 * m
turns = R / z
holes = int((turns - 1) * H)
print(round(d, 3))
print(round(p, 3))
print(round(a, 3))
print(round(b, 3))
print(round(da, 3))
print(round(turns, 3))
print(holes)

traps: Module is the pitch diameter per tooth in mm; diametral pitch is the inch-based reciprocal. Do not mix them in one calculation.
The form cutter number depends on tooth count. One arbitrary cutter gives the wrong involute for another z.
Hobbing is generation, not forming. Conventional and climb are hobbing types; they are not forming methods.
For indexing, multiply the fractional crank turn by the chosen hole-circle count, not by 40.
Axial feed and radial feed are hobbing feed directions; they are not the same as conventional and climb hobbing.

quiz.q: Define module and give its unit.
quiz.a: Module m = d/z, where d is pitch diameter in mm and z is tooth count. Its unit is mm per tooth.

quiz.q: Why does one form cutter not cut all tooth counts correctly?
quiz.a: The involute shape changes with tooth count z. A cutter set covers ranges of z, and the nearest cutter number is used.

quiz.q: A spur gear has 40 teeth and module 2 mm. Find pitch diameter, circular pitch and outside diameter.
quiz.a: d = mz = 2 × 40 = 80 mm. p = πm = 6.283 mm. Outside diameter = d + 2m = 84 mm.

quiz.q: Compare hobbing and form milling for 5000 spur gears.
quiz.a: Hobbing is continuous generation: accurate spacing and fast production. Form milling copies each gap and indexes every tooth; it is slower and depends on cutter number, so it suits small batches.

quiz.q: Name two hobbing types by cutter rotation and two hobbing feed directions.
quiz.a: By cutter rotation: conventional and climb. Feed directions: axial and radial.

quiz.q: Index 36 teeth with a 40:1 dividing head on an 18-hole circle.
quiz.a: Crank turns = 40/36 = 1 1/9 turn. Holes = (1/9) × 18 = 2 holes. Use 1 full turn plus 2 holes on the 18-hole circle.

quiz.q: Why does climb hobbing often give better finish?
quiz.a: The cutter runs with the feed, so chip thickness starts high and falls, reducing rubbing. On a rigid machine with backlash removed, this gives better finish than conventional hobbing.

beyond: Not for the exam. CNC gear hobbing with an electronic gearbox removes change gears and allows diagonal feed and tooth-flank modification. Dry hobbing uses coated carbide and air or oil mist instead of flood coolant. Gear skiving cuts internal and near-shoulder gears with a pinion cutter at high speed. Search terms: electronic gearbox hobbing, gear skiving, topological modification, dry hobbing.
